events.content: Stage 'positions_and_core_issues' begins
Absent active concessions, positions harden and a trilateral package drifts further away.
With the U.S.-Mexico bilateral already in place, Canada is pressured to concede to join the package.
Weak labor enforcement hardens domestic opposition.

  ustr: Look, Mexico just signed off on 75% regional value content and a wage-floor component — that's the floor for this deal, not the ceiling. Canada can match it or explain to your industry why you got left out of the largest auto market in North America. What's your opening on autos and enforceable labor standards?
  canada_min: We can work with 75% RVC if the labor value content is genuinely enforceable — not just window-dressing. But I need clarity: does Mexico's wage floor apply to all three countries, or just Mexico? Because if Canada's auto workers subsidize a two-tier system, that doesn't fly domestically, and you know it.
  canada_min: Fair point on the market size — we're not walking away. But the wage-floor answer matters more than the RVC number itself. If it's Mexico-only, we need a different path: either a genuine North American wage floor all three countries commit to, or a labor-enforcement mechanism with real inspection teeth that applies equally. Which are you prepared to table?
  ustr: The wage floor applies to all three countries — same standard, same enforcement. But here's the deal: you get real inspections with surprise audits and trade-remedy teeth, or you get a higher RVC number to compensate. Pick one, because we're not doing both. Mexico's already accepted this framework, and frankly, we've got a bilateral that works without you.
  mexico_neg: Look, the wage floor is the same for all three — that's settled. But Canada's point on enforcement is fair: we don't need U.S. inspectors in our factories. How about this: joint Mexico-Canada labor audits, and the U.S. gets trade-remedy access if either of us fails? We sign this week, and we move forward together.
  us_congress: USTR, I hear Mexico and Canada on joint audits — that works. But "trade-remedy access" doesn't mean anything in a legal text. If a joint audit finds a violation, what happens? Tariffs? Suspension of benefits? And who decides, how fast? Congress needs to see real enforcement language, not a framework. What's the actual remedy if Mexico or Canada blows through the wage floor?
  auto_industry: Congress, real quick — if a joint audit flags a wage violation, are we talking automatic tariffs, suspension of that product line, or suspension of the whole agreement? And who triggers the remedy — the country where the violation happened, or the injured party? Because my members need to know: does a finding in Mexico shut down their Canadian parts plant, or just that supplier? That's the difference between workable and catastrophic.
  us_congress: Look, it's got to be automatic and targeted — a violation at a specific facility triggers suspension of benefits for that producer and its direct supply chain, not the whole agreement. That's the only way Congress votes yes: real consequences that actually bite, but don't crater the entire deal if one plant screws up. And the injured country files the complaint; we don't need a three-country committee deciding for weeks while violations pile up.
  labor_union: Mexico, joint audits sound workable — but you're saying Mexico-Canada panels decide violations together? That means Canada's labor board and your labor authorities have to agree before the injured party can file a remedy claim. That's a veto point.   supply_chain_mfr: USTR, I hear you on labor teeth and auto rules — that's workable for my members. But here's what freezes investment: nobody's said whether this deal auto-sunsets in five years or stays open. What's the U.S. position on renewal versus termination, and is there room for a rolling review instead?
